title: Edge predictive-maintenance pilot for manufacturing plants
description: A manufacturer operates twelve plants with mixed generations of pumps, motors, and packaging equipment. Maintenance is primarily calendar-based, while unexpected failures create lost production and emergency repair costs. The company wants to test predictive maintenance, but connectivity, sensor quality, and historical maintenance records differ substantially between plants.
objective: Choose a safe pilot architecture and rollout plan that can demonstrate measurable maintenance value before any enterprise-wide commitment.
constraints: The pilot must produce an evidence-based go or no-go recommendation within nine months.
The pilot may include at most three plants and 120 monitored assets.
No model or analytics component may directly control production equipment during the pilot.
Production networks must remain isolated from inbound public internet connections.
Local data collection must continue during connectivity losses of at least 48 hours.
Installation may require no more than two hours of planned downtime per monitored asset.
The total pilot budget is limited to 450000 euros, including sensors, integration, and training.
Maintenance technicians must be able to inspect the evidence behind every generated alert.
Raw high-frequency vibration data may leave a plant only after information-security approval.
The pilot must not replace the existing safety inspection schedule.
context: Three plants have reliable fiber connectivity, six have intermittent wide-area connectivity, and three exchange operational data only through scheduled transfers.
Existing programmable logic controllers expose different industrial protocols and some are no longer supported by their vendors.
Fourteen months of maintenance work orders are available, but failure codes and asset identifiers are inconsistent across plants.
A previous sensor trial covered ten motors for eight weeks and did not include confirmed bearing failures.
The central data team has Python and time-series analytics experience but no production machine-learning operations platform.
Plant technicians already use a computerized maintenance management system for work orders.
Potential approaches include edge-only rules, edge feature extraction with centralized analytics, and centralized ingestion of raw sensor streams.
The financial cost of one hour of lost production has not been normalized across candidate plants.
stated_facts: Historical work-order labels are inconsistent between plants.
The earlier sensor trial contained no confirmed bearing-failure example.
Three plants cannot continuously transmit operational data to a central service.
The existing maintenance system remains the authoritative source for work orders.
Pilot analytics are advisory and cannot operate production equipment.
